title: Frederick Douglass Remembers His Mother
text:
Frederick Douglass was born into slavery in Talbot County, Maryland, around 1818. In the first chapter of his autobiography, published in 1845, he described how he and his mother were separated when he was a baby, as was common, he said, in that part of Maryland: children were taken from their mothers to blunt the natural bond between them.

His mother, Harriet Bailey, was hired out to a farmer about twelve miles away. Douglass wrote that he saw her only four or five times in his life, and always at night. After a full day's work in the fields, she would walk the twelve miles on foot to see him, lie down with him and get him to sleep. Before he woke in the morning, she was gone, because she had to be back in the field at sunrise, and a slave not there in time could be whipped.

She died when he was about seven. He was not allowed to be with her during her illness or at her burial. He wrote that he received the news of her death with much the same feelings as he would the death of a stranger, because he had hardly known her.

In a later autobiography, written ten years after, Douglass added one more memory of her standing up for him against a cruel cook, and wrote that he learned only later that his mother had been able to read.
lesson: Love can find a way even under brutal conditions, sometimes at enormous personal cost. The effort a parent makes to be present is never wasted.
source: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (1845), chapter 1; My Bondage and My Freedom (1855)
